Zemu Gap Peak.notable: A subsidiary summit of the Kangchenjunga massif rather than an independent mountain; no known attempts.

Chiumo.notable: No documented ascent; recent attempts have come from the south.

Nanda Khat.notable: Sources give different first-ascent years; 1972 is the most cited.

Chombu.notable: No documented ascent. British attempts in 2019 and 2022 turned back; climbing is tightly controlled near the Tibet border.

Hanuman Tibba.first_ascent_by: Bruce's guide Führer and party (recorded in the Himalayan Journal, 1964)
Hanuman Tibba.notable: Called the 'Solang Weisshorn' in early accounts; published heights range from 5,860 m to 5,982 m. Wikipedia calls it the highest peak of Kangra district.

Stok Kangri.status_note: Closed: the All Ladakh Tour Operators Association stopped climbs from 2020 (over-tourism, Stok village water source, glacier retreat); on 21 Dec 2023 the Ladakh administration closed 'all kinds of expeditions' with immediate effect, citing depletion of the Stok glacier. No reopening found as of Oct 2026.

Deo Tibba.first_ascent_by: J. de V. Graaff's party (sources differ on who else was in it)
Deo Tibba.difficulty_note: Flat snow-dome summit, but the approach crosses the steep Duhangan Col and a crevassed glacier on fixed ropes
Deo Tibba.notable: First climbed in 1952 by J. de V. Graaff's party via the Duhangan col between Deo Tibba and Indrasan. Wikipedia names Clare Graaff and Pasang Dawa Lama; the Himalayan Journal names Graaff, his wife and K. E. Berrill.

Mount Yunam.difficulty_note: Non-technical but steep: scree, moraine and snow slopes of about 50° near the top; altitude is the main challenge
Mount Yunam.notable: Climbed from the Bharatpur tent camp on the Manali–Leh highway; summit day is a long single push. No documented first ascent found.

Mentok Kangri.difficulty_note: Non-technical in normal conditions: snow slopes early in the season, loose moraine and rock scrambling when dry; the massif has several summits (Mentok I–III) whose names and heights differ between maps
Mentok Kangri.notable: Rises above the west shore of Tso Moriri; the lake is ringed by 6,000 m peaks including Mentok Kangri and Lungser Kangri. A 2010s SummitPost report gives about 6,250 m for Mentok I and a GPS reading of 6,151 m on a lower summit.

Ladakhi Peak.notable: Climbed from Beas Kund above Solang; the final ridge is narrow and exposed, so it 'can feel like a mountain' despite the trekking-peak label. Published heights vary (about 5,257–5,345 m).

Reo Purgyil.first_ascent_by: Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP records list the 1971 climb as Leo Pargial; a 1991 Indian team found an 'ITBP EXP 1971' cairn on the 6,816 m summit)
Reo Purgyil.status_note: Climbed; open (no closure found, Oct 2026). Border belt beyond Jangi: foreigners need a Protected Area Permit, Indians need none. An ITBP team summited on 16 Sep 2026 (reported height 6,759 m).
Reo Purgyil.difficulty_note: Remote border massif: scree approach from Nako, then a glacier and a long, loose west ridge with short rock pitches near the top (HJ 48, 1991)
Reo Purgyil.notable: Highest peak of Himachal Pradesh. Twin of Leo Pargial (6,791 m), about 2 km to the north; Nako village is the trekking base.

Kangto.status_note: First recorded ascent: an 18-member Indian Army team (4 Corps) reached the summit on 26 Nov 2025 (Arunachal Governor's press release, 8 Dec 2025). An ITBP/IMF team reached the approach in 2017. Border area near the McMahon Line.

Nanda Devi.status_note: Nanda Devi Sanctuary and main summit closed to climbers and locals since 1983 (one-off 1993 army clean-up and summit). In July 2025 the IMF's reopening proposal went to Uttarakhand Tourism for review; no reopening order found as of Oct 2026. Feb 2026 Uttarakhand opening of 83 peaks named Nanda Devi East, not the main summit.

Kangchenjunga.notable: India's highest peak and world's 3rd highest; second ascent 31 May 1977 by an Indian Army team (leader Col. Narendra Kumar) via the NE spur from Sikkim. In May 2025 Indian Army teams summited from Nepal; Sikkim's Chief Minister then asked the Centre to stop expeditions from the Nepal side too.

Kanamo.status_note: Access status unclear (as of Oct 2026): on 20 Jul 2019 the village leaders above Kibber barred all trekking groups after trekkers contaminated a water source; no official lifting order has been found. A local Spiti climber reached the summit in 2026 (Tribune, 4 Jul 2026) and operators advertise 2026 departures, but no district or state order confirming open access was found — check with the Kibber panchayat / Kaza administration before booking.
Kanamo.notable: Non-technical walk-up above Kibber in the Kibber Wildlife Sanctuary area; heights quoted 5,964–5,974 m. In 2026 Tenzin Norden became the first woman from Spiti to summit it (Tribune, 4 Jul 2026).

Chau Chau Kang Nilda.first_ascent_by: J.O.M. Roberts (1939, while crossing Spiti from Kullu)
Chau Chau Kang Nilda.base: Kaza → Langza (about 4,420 m); base camp above Langza
Chau Chau Kang Nilda.difficulty_note: Glaciated dome NE of Kaza; normal route by the south-west ridge / scree slopes with two high camps
Chau Chau Kang Nilda.notable: 'Blue moon in the sky'; also called Guan Nelda. Second ascent 1955 (Trevor Braham and Peter Holmes); Indian ascents 1966 and 1981; a Calcutta team made the first ascent of the south-east ridge on 15 September (AAJ 1991).

Mulkila.first_ascent_by: Ludwig Krenek, Robey Johnson & Fritz Kolb (Anglo-Austrian expedition)
Mulkila.difficulty_note: Crevassed Milang Glacier and a narrow icefall to a high cwm; the summit is gained by the steep, loose rock of the south ridge (1939 route) or the south-west face
Mulkila.base: Darcha (3,360 m) → Milang valley; base camp on the Milang Glacier moraine
Mulkila.notable: Highest peak of Lahaul and an Ultra (prominence 1,586 m); also called M4, its name is translated as 'Silver God'. First climbed 7 Sep 1939; first Indian ascent 22 Aug 1989 (Goutam Dutta & R.S. Negi).

Indrasan.first_ascent_by: Kyoto University Alpine Club (Japan): Kojiro Tomita & Yasumasa Miyaki
Indrasan.difficulty_note: Considered the hardest peak of the Pir Panjal: icefall, steep ice and a rock band on the final peak; later lines include the West and East ridges
Indrasan.base: Manali → Jagatsukh / Duhangan valley (the 1962 team came up the Malana Glacier)
Indrasan.notable: First climbed 13 Oct 1962 by Tomita and Miyaki of the Kyoto University Alpine Club, on the same day their teammates made the second ascent of Deo Tibba. Name: 'Indra' + 'Aasana', the seat of Lord Indra.

Satopanth.base: Gangotri → Gaumukh → Nandanvan → Vasuki Tal (base camp)
Satopanth.notable: First climbed 1 Aug 1947 by a Swiss team (Roch, Dittert, Graven, Sutter), 15 days before Indian independence; second-highest peak of Gangotri National Park. The usual line is the north-east ridge from Vasuki Tal, with a long corniced crest.

Kang Yatse I.first_ascent_by: Simon Fraser, Mark Dravers & Mike Ritchie (British; 'probably the first ascent', AAJ 2023)
Kang Yatse I.base: Chilling → Markha valley → Nimaling, or Shang Sumdo → Gongmaru La
Kang Yatse I.notable: True (east) summit of the Kang Yatse massif; 23 Aug 1977 via an east-side couloir and the south ridge. First traverse from Kang Yatse II by HMI instructors, 17 Aug 2018.

Shivling.first_ascent_by: ITBP team led by Hukam Singh (3 Jun 1974, west ridge)
Shivling.difficulty_note: Steep twin-summited rock/ice peak; easiest line (west ridge, the 1974 route) is long, technical and threatened by a serac barrier
Shivling.notable: Iconic 'Matterhorn of the Himalaya' above Gaumukh; at least ten routes, incl. the 1981 East Ridge and 1993 North Pillar. SW summit 6,501 m.

Trisul I.first_ascent_by: Tom Longstaff with Alexis & Henri Brocherel and Karbir (Burathoki), 12 Jun 1907
Trisul I.notable: First 7,000 m summit ever climbed (12 Jun 1907), via the Rishi Ganga, Trisul glacier and NE flank; the highest summit reached until Pauhunri (1911) and the first major climb to use supplementary oxygen. Modern standard route: Sutol road-head, Hom Kund base camp and the west ridge. On 1 Oct 2021 an avalanche at about 6,700 m killed four Indian Navy climbers.

Sickle Moon.notable: Highest summit of the Kishtwar Himalaya (also called Bharanzar); first climbed in 1975 by an Indian Army HAWS team.
